assumed_stack: Java 21, Spring Boot 3.x, Spring Framework 6.x; imperative proxy-based Spring unless stated otherwise
evidence_notice: All entries are E0 unverified interview patterns. Frequency, round and level are editorial estimates. No company attribution or website verification is claimed.

questions.question: What does Spring's container actually do when it injects a service dependency?
questions.answer: The container reads bean definitions, determines how each object should be constructed, resolves its required collaborators and manages the resulting instances according to their scopes. With constructor injection, my service declares its dependencies as constructor parameters and Spring supplies matching managed objects. Those collaborators may be proxies rather than raw implementation instances. The benefit is that object construction and configuration are separated from business behavior; the service does not have to locate or instantiate its dependencies itself. In a unit test I can construct it directly with test doubles. Injection does not make the service thread-safe or eliminate the need to choose appropriate interfaces, lifetimes and ownership boundaries.

followups.q: Is dependency injection exclusive to Spring?
followups.a: No. Passing collaborators through a constructor is dependency injection even when ordinary Java code constructs the objects.

followups.q: What differs from a service locator?
followups.a: With injection the required collaborators are supplied explicitly; with a locator the object looks them up, often hiding dependencies from its constructor.

questions.trap: Describing dependency injection only as adding @Autowired, without explaining who constructs and connects the objects.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: Why prefer constructor injection for required dependencies over field injection?
questions.answer: Constructor injection makes the object's required collaborators visible and available before it can be used. The fields can be final, and a test can instantiate the service without starting Spring or using reflection to populate hidden fields. Field injection happens after construction, so a constructor cannot safely use those injected fields and the class is harder to create correctly outside the container. Setter injection can suit a genuinely optional or replaceable collaborator, but I would not hide a required dependency that way. A class with many constructor parameters is also useful design feedback: it may have too many responsibilities. Constructor injection exposes that coupling rather than causing it.

followups.q: Does a single constructor need @Autowired?
followups.a: For an ordinary Spring-managed bean with one constructor, Spring can use it without the annotation.

followups.q: Does final make a collaborator immutable?
followups.a: No. It prevents reassignment of the reference, not mutation of the collaborator itself.

questions.trap: Claiming field injection is necessary for mocking, or that a final dependency reference makes the dependency thread-safe.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; estimates only.

questions.question: How do @Component, @Service, @Repository and @Bean differ?
questions.answer: Component scanning can discover classes marked with @Component or stereotypes built on it. @Service expresses a service-layer role; it does not automatically create a transaction. @Repository expresses a persistence role and can participate in persistence-exception translation when the relevant infrastructure is configured. @Bean instead declares a factory method whose returned object the container manages. I use it when I need explicit construction or cannot annotate the class, such as a library client. These registration mechanisms still produce bean definitions with scope, lifecycle and dependency rules. Adding several stereotypes does not create extra architectural behavior by itself; I check what infrastructure actually processes each annotation.

followups.q: Does @Repository catch every database exception?
followups.a: No. Translation depends on configured post-processors and applicable persistence exceptions; the annotation is not a universal try/catch.

followups.q: Can a @Bean method accept dependencies as arguments?
followups.a: Yes. The container resolves its parameters, which is a clear way to wire factory-created objects.

questions.trap: Saying @Service automatically makes methods transactional or @Repository alone implements data access.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; no reuse of earlier off-allowlist interview evidence.

questions.question: Two beans implement the same interface. How do you make injection deterministic?
questions.answer: I would decide whether the consumer needs one preferred implementation, a particular role, or every implementation. @Primary can establish the preferred candidate for a single-valued dependency. A qualifier narrows the eligible candidates at the injection point, which is better when the choice has business meaning such as read versus write access. If the consumer dispatches among several connector strategies, injecting a collection or map of implementations can make that explicit. I avoid relying on accidental names or registration order. Qualifiers do not bypass type compatibility, and @Primary is not a rule to remove all other implementations from collection injection. The wiring should remain understandable when a new implementation is added.

followups.q: What happens with no unique candidate?
followups.a: Resolution can fail with a no-unique-bean error; inspect the injection point and candidate definitions rather than adding annotations at random.

followups.q: Does @Primary filter an injected list down to one bean?
followups.a: No. A list can contain all eligible matching beans; primary selection addresses single-valued resolution.

questions.trap: Using @Primary to hide an architectural choice that differs between consumers.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; proposed connector dispatch is not a claim about Harsh's current wiring. Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 5.3 (Yash, EY).

questions.question: Why does a prototype bean injected into a singleton often appear to behave like a singleton?
questions.answer: Prototype scope creates a new instance for each container request for that bean. If Spring constructs a singleton and resolves its prototype dependency once, the singleton keeps that particular reference. Calling the singleton repeatedly does not repeat dependency resolution. If a fresh collaborator is genuinely needed per operation, I can inject ObjectProvider and request an instance at the required boundary, or use another explicit factory mechanism. A scoped proxy can also defer target resolution according to scope, but I need to understand that behavior rather than assume every field access creates a new object. Prototype objects also require cleanup ownership: Spring does not normally manage their full destruction lifecycle after handing them to the caller.

followups.q: Is Spring singleton one instance for the entire JVM?
followups.a: No. It is per bean definition within a container; separate application contexts can have separate instances.

followups.q: When is request scope more appropriate?
followups.a: When the state belongs to one web request and the application has a supported active request context.

questions.trap: Assuming prototype means Spring replaces a singleton's injected field on every method call.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; scope resolution rather than singleton thread safety in S05.

questions.question: What is the practical difference between a constructor, @PostConstruct and an application runner?
questions.answer: The constructor establishes the object's required state from its constructor dependencies; field or setter injection has not happened yet. @PostConstruct is an initialization callback after dependency population, but it is still part of bean creation, not proof that the whole application is ready for traffic. I would not rely on calling my own proxied methods there to activate advice. ApplicationRunner or CommandLineRunner runs later during Spring Boot startup after context refresh and before startup is reported ready. A failing runner can fail startup. I keep initialization bounded and decide whether an unavailable downstream should prevent startup or merely affect readiness, rather than placing an indefinite network wait into bean construction.

followups.q: Which annotation namespace applies here?
followups.a: For the assumed Spring Boot 3 stack, use jakarta.annotation.PostConstruct rather than the old javax annotation namespace.

followups.q: Should a runner start an untracked forever-thread?
followups.a: No. Long-running workers need explicit lifecycle and shutdown ownership instead of detached startup work.

questions.trap: Equating successful construction of one bean with full application readiness or completed proxy setup.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; Java 21 / Boot 3 / Framework 6 assumptions.

questions.question: How does a Spring AOP proxy make an annotation such as @Transactional take effect?
questions.answer: In proxy-based Spring AOP, callers receive a wrapper that intercepts eligible method calls and applies an interceptor chain around the target invocation. For transactional advice, that chain consults transaction metadata and coordinates the configured transaction manager before and after the business method. The annotation is metadata; it does not rewrite every call in the JVM. An invocation must reach the proxy and an interceptable method for the advice to run. This explains why manually constructing the class or calling a method directly from another method on the same target can bypass the advice. I would debug the actual injected object, call boundary and configuration before blaming the database or adding more annotations.

followups.q: Does new Service() get Spring advice?
followups.a: Not merely because its class has annotations. An ordinary manually constructed object is outside the container's proxying process.

followups.q: Is this the same as AspectJ weaving?
followups.a: No. Weaving can instrument other join points; this answer is specifically about proxy-based Spring AOP.

questions.trap: Saying the annotation itself opens a transaction regardless of how the method is invoked.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; GAP follows the explicitly supplied Spring proxies gap.

questions.question: What changes between interface-based and class-based Spring proxies, especially for final or private methods?
questions.answer: A JDK dynamic proxy implements interfaces and intercepts calls through those interfaces; it is not an instance of the concrete implementation class. A class-based proxy subclasses the target type, so it needs an extensible class and methods it can override. A final class cannot be subclass-proxied, and final or private methods cannot be overridden for class-based interception. That does not mean a final implementation method can never be advised through an interface proxy: the interface call is intercepted before delegation. I would check the configured proxy strategy and injection type rather than assume one mechanism universally. Method-visibility support also depends on the particular advice and framework version, so public service boundaries remain the clearest default.

followups.q: Why can injection by concrete type fail?
followups.a: An interface proxy is not assignable to its target implementation class; depend on the interface or deliberately configure an appropriate proxy mechanism.

followups.q: Does class-based proxying fix self-invocation?
followups.a: Not in the ordinary Spring proxy call model. Internal calls on the target still bypass the external proxy boundary.

questions.trap: Claiming final methods can never be advised under any proxy mechanism, or class-based proxies make private methods interceptable.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; GAP follows Spring proxies. No blanket claim about non-public method advice is made.

questions.question: A transaction annotation works when another bean calls the method, but not from a method in the same class. How would you repair the boundary?
questions.answer: The external caller goes through the proxy, whereas the internal call normally executes directly on the target. I first clarify the intended transaction boundary. If the whole use case should be atomic, placing the boundary on the externally invoked orchestration method may be correct. If the inner operation needs independently applied behavior, I can move it to a separate injected collaborator so the call crosses a proxy, or use explicit programmatic transaction management where it improves clarity. I avoid changing propagation settings until I have fixed the invocation path, because ignored metadata cannot change anything. An integration test should observe the database outcome on both success and failure rather than merely check for the annotation.

followups.q: Will REQUIRES_NEW alone fix an internal call?
followups.a: No. The interceptor must run before propagation metadata can have any effect.

followups.q: Should you always inject the bean into itself?
followups.a: No. It adds wiring and lifecycle complexity; a clearer responsibility boundary or programmatic API is usually easier to reason about.

questions.trap: Changing annotation parameters without checking whether the invocation reaches the advice at all.
questions.notes: Unverified repair scenario; complements proxy mechanics in 007 instead of repeating the definition.

questions.question: Two constructor-injected services depend on each other. Why does startup fail, and is enabling circular references the right fix?
questions.answer: Spring cannot finish constructing either object when each constructor requires the other completed instance first. I would examine why the responsibilities depend in both directions: often an orchestration service or a smaller shared collaborator can remove the cycle. Spring Boot 3 disallows circular references by default. Enabling the setting is not a general solution to an eager constructor cycle; some setter-based singleton cycles can use early references, but those introduce initialization and proxy hazards. Lazy indirection or a provider can defer a dependency when that lifetime is genuinely intended, yet it can also postpone the failure until the first call. I prefer making the dependency graph coherent rather than merely getting startup past the error.

followups.q: Would changing both dependencies to fields prove the design is fixed?
followups.a: No. It changes construction timing and may conceal the cycle without resolving responsibility or initialization problems.

followups.q: When can ObjectProvider help legitimately?
followups.a: When deferred or optional lookup reflects the real lifecycle, and the first lookup does not recreate the same unresolved construction cycle.

questions.trap: Treating allow-circular-references as a universal repair for mutually required constructor dependencies.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; GAP follows the explicit circular-dependency assessment.

questions.question: Why can calling another @Bean method behave differently with proxyBeanMethods=false?
questions.answer: In full configuration mode, Spring enhances a @Configuration class so interceptable calls between its @Bean methods can be routed through the container and respect the bean's scope. With proxyBeanMethods=false, ordinary Java calls between those methods are no longer intercepted in that way. A direct call can construct an extra object rather than obtain the managed singleton, depending on the method body. I prefer expressing the dependency as a @Bean method parameter: Spring resolves that parameter, so construction does not depend on direct inter-method calls. Disabling method proxying can be appropriate when bean methods are independent, but it is not a harmless switch if existing code relies on the interception semantics.

followups.q: Is this ordinary service AOP proxying?
followups.a: No. Configuration-class enhancement has a specific role in managing bean-method calls; do not equate every Spring proxy mechanism.

followups.q: Can the extra object miss lifecycle processing?
followups.a: Yes. An object created by an ordinary direct Java call is not automatically the registered bean instance with its full container processing.

questions.trap: Assuming every call to a method annotated @Bean is automatically a lookup in the container.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; GAP relates to proxy mechanism understanding. Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 5.4 (Yash).

questions.question: What is the difference between BeanFactoryPostProcessor and BeanPostProcessor?
questions.answer: A BeanFactoryPostProcessor works on container metadata, typically modifying bean definitions before ordinary beans are instantiated. A BeanPostProcessor works on bean instances around initialization and may return a wrapped instance, which is how important container behavior such as proxy creation can be integrated. The distinction is definition versus object. I would not call getBean casually from a factory post-processor, because early creation can prevent that bean from receiving the complete later processing pipeline. Ordering also matters: some processors run before others, and making a processor depend on many application services can pull those services into creation too early. I use these extension points only when ordinary configuration cannot express the requirement.

followups.q: Can a BeanPostProcessor replace the reference callers receive?
followups.a: Yes. It can return a wrapper, which is why the injected object need not be the raw target instance.

followups.q: Is a post-processor just an application startup callback?
followups.a: No. It participates in container construction semantics; use runners or lifecycle events for ordinary startup work.

questions.trap: Using a factory post-processor to eagerly fetch application beans without considering incomplete lifecycle processing.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; frequency, round and level are estimates.

questions.question: What does Spring Boot auto-configuration decide, and how does it back off when you define a bean?
questions.answer: Boot imports candidate configuration classes and evaluates conditions against the classpath, configuration properties, application type and existing bean definitions. Matching configurations contribute sensible default beans. Conditions such as missing-bean checks let particular defaults back off when the application supplies the relevant collaborator. Backoff is specific to the condition: defining any arbitrary bean does not disable all auto-configuration, and declaring a bean with the same name is not the same mechanism as satisfying a missing-type condition. I would inspect which configuration matched and why rather than describe Boot as guessing. Starters mainly supply a dependency set that makes useful configurations applicable; they are not themselves a replacement for the container.

followups.q: Does component scanning discover all Boot auto-configuration?
followups.a: No. Auto-configuration has a separate import mechanism; application component scanning and auto-configuration selection serve different roles.

followups.q: Should excluding a configuration be the first response to startup failure?
followups.a: No. Inspect its conditions and the failing dependency first; exclusion can conceal missing or contradictory configuration.

questions.trap: Saying Boot always overrides user configuration or that every custom bean disables all defaults.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; Boot 3 assumptions.

questions.question: When is @ConfigurationProperties preferable to scattered @Value fields?
questions.answer: For a related group of settings, @ConfigurationProperties gives a typed object with structured binding, conversion and a clear prefix. I can represent timeouts as durations and nested configuration as nested objects instead of spreading string placeholders across services. Validation can reject missing or invalid settings at startup when the configuration bean is registered and the required validation infrastructure is present. Immutable constructor-bound settings also make ownership clear. @Value is useful for a small individual expression or property, but it is less convenient for a coherent configuration model. Neither mechanism makes secrets safe to log, and binding successfully is not proof that the chosen operational values are sensible for the workload.

followups.q: Does placing @ConfigurationProperties on a class always register it?
followups.a: No. Use an appropriate registration mechanism such as configuration-properties scanning or explicit enablement.

followups.q: What should a missing critical secret do?
followups.a: Fail through an explicit safe validation path without printing the secret or silently using an insecure default.

questions.trap: Treating successful string injection as equivalent to a validated configuration model.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; no configuration snippet is claimed to have executed. Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 5.5 (Yash).

questions.question: A service uses the wrong endpoint in production despite a correct application file. How would you trace the effective setting?
questions.answer: I would inspect the effective environment rather than only the packaged configuration file. Active profiles, external configuration, environment variables, system properties and command-line arguments can contribute or override values according to Boot's property-source rules. I check how the setting was bound and trace its origin through available diagnostic information, taking care not to expose credentials. Profiles can select beans or configuration, but they do not create security boundaries and activating a profile does not guarantee every required setting is valid. I would compare the running deployment's inputs with the intended release configuration and add a focused configuration test for the relevant combination instead of editing a file the process is not actually using.

followups.q: Should environment diagnostic endpoints be public?
followups.a: No. Restrict management access and verify sanitization; configuration diagnostics can reveal sensitive operational information.

followups.q: Can two profiles activate conflicting beans?
followups.a: Yes. Profiles select definitions; they do not automatically resolve ambiguity between simultaneously active candidates.

questions.trap: Assuming the value in the repository's application file must be the value used by the running process.
questions.notes: Unverified diagnostic pattern, not a fabricated incident story. Exact full property-source ordering is not asserted.

questions.question: A Boot application fails because a required bean is missing. What is your debugging sequence?
questions.answer: I begin with the failing injection point and its most specific cause, not only the outer context-startup exception. Then I check whether the expected definition exists: is its package scanned, its configuration imported, its profile active, and its required dependency present? If auto-configuration should supply it, I inspect the condition evaluation report to see why that configuration matched or backed off. If a definition exists but creation failed, I follow that creation failure rather than treating it as a discovery problem. I also consider qualifier and proxy-type mismatches. Finally I reproduce the smallest relevant context in a test, which is more informative than repeatedly starting the entire service with arbitrary annotations added.

followups.q: Why can moving the main application class break discovery?
followups.a: The default scan boundary is influenced by its package; moving it can leave application components outside that boundary.

followups.q: Does lazy initialization fix missing dependencies?
followups.a: It can defer a failure until first use, but does not supply the missing collaborator or make the wiring correct.

questions.trap: Treating every UnsatisfiedDependencyException as a missing @Component instead of following the underlying cause.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; no new code snippets. Section remains incomplete.

questions.question: Does publishing a Spring application event automatically run listeners asynchronously or durably?
questions.answer: Not by default. With the ordinary default event multicaster, listeners run synchronously on the publisher's thread. A slow listener delays publishing, and an uncaught listener exception can propagate to the publisher unless the configured delivery mechanism handles it differently. Asynchronous delivery requires deliberate configuration and an explicit failure-handling policy. Neither choice turns an in-memory application event into durable messaging: a process failure can lose work, and another service replica does not automatically receive the event. I use local events to decouple components when that delivery contract is sufficient. For work that must survive a crash or cross process boundaries, I need a durable mechanism and a strategy for coordinating it with business-state changes.

followups.q: Does returning from publishEvent prove a remote consumer processed anything?
followups.a: No. Local publication has no such remote delivery or processing guarantee.

followups.q: Can an async listener use the publisher's transaction automatically?
followups.a: Not for ordinary thread-bound imperative transactions. Moving execution to another thread does not transfer that transaction.

questions.trap: Replacing a durable queue with application events because the API also uses the word publish.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. All frequency, round and level labels are estimates. Default imperative event configuration assumed.

questions.question: What does @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) guarantee, and what does it not guarantee?
questions.answer: It ties listener execution to the successful commit phase of the transaction associated with event publication, rather than running the listener immediately. For ordinary imperative transactions, if no transaction exists the listener is not invoked unless fallback execution is enabled. After-commit timing is useful, but it is not durable delivery: the process can fail after the database commits and before follow-up work completes. A listener failure cannot undo that already committed transaction. Database writes from an after-commit callback also need an intentional new transaction boundary; the old resources may still be accessible even though their transaction is finished. If losing the follow-up is unacceptable, an outbox written in the original transaction is a more appropriate starting point.

followups.q: Does AFTER_COMMIT mean async?
followups.a: No. Phase and execution thread are separate concerns; after-commit listeners are not automatically background jobs.

followups.q: Can the caller safely retry the whole operation after a listener error?
followups.a: Not without reconciling the committed outcome. The business write may already have succeeded, so retrying can duplicate it.

questions.trap: Treating an after-commit callback as an atomic, durable extension of the transaction that already completed.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. Imperative transaction assumptions; full distributed outbox design belongs in S08/S13.

questions.question: Should a temporary database outage make a Spring Boot service fail its liveness check?
questions.answer: Usually not. Liveness asks whether this process is in a state where restarting it is useful. Restarting every replica because a shared database is unavailable can create a restart storm without repairing the dependency. Readiness asks whether this instance should receive traffic, so a required dependency can be relevant there, depending on whether the service has useful degraded behavior. I would define the health groups deliberately instead of pointing every probe at one aggregate health endpoint. Startup checks need a separate allowance for initialization time. I would also verify that the probed listener represents the actual serving path, since a separate management port can respond while the main request path is unhealthy.

followups.q: Should every optional dependency affect readiness?
followups.a: No. Removing otherwise useful instances from service can worsen an outage; decide which dependencies are essential to the advertised traffic contract.

followups.q: Does a successful health endpoint prove all requests will succeed?
followups.a: No. It is a limited observation of configured health criteria, not an end-to-end guarantee for every workload.

questions.trap: Using dependency availability as a universal reason to restart the application.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; no blanket claim about default endpoint exposure or included health indicators.

questions.question: When would SmartLifecycle be more suitable than starting a worker in @PostConstruct?
questions.answer: SmartLifecycle gives a managed component explicit start, stop and running-state behavior, plus phase-based coordination with other lifecycle components. That is useful for a long-lived consumer or dispatcher whose operation must begin and end in an orderly way. Lower phases generally start earlier and higher phases stop earlier, subject to dependency relationships. Its callback-based stop contract allows asynchronous stopping, but the component must invoke the supplied callback when stopping is actually complete so the lifecycle processor can progress. Starting a detached thread during bean initialization has no equivalent coordination by itself. I would keep startup bounded, make stopping idempotent, and define what happens when draining exceeds the configured shutdown budget.

followups.q: Should the stop callback run before workers stop?
followups.a: No. It signals completed stopping; reporting completion prematurely can let dependencies shut down while workers still use them.

followups.q: Does this replace all resource cleanup?
followups.a: No. Lifecycle stopping and destruction need coherent ownership; resources still require cleanup appropriate to their actual lifetime.

questions.trap: Starting an unmanaged background thread during initialization and assuming the container will infer how to drain it.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; proposed lifecycle usage, not a claim about Harsh's implementation.

questions.question: Does @Order on two services force their singleton beans to initialize in that order?
questions.answer: No. @Order participates in supported ordering contracts, such as sorting injected collections or ordering particular extension points. It is not a general singleton construction sequence. If one bean genuinely requires another collaborator, that dependency should be explicit in the wiring. @DependsOn can express an initialization dependency that is not represented by an injected reference, but using it everywhere can hide a confused design. Startup runners have their own ordering support, and lifecycle components use phase coordination. I would first identify whether the requirement concerns object creation, execution of startup tasks, ordered strategy selection or shutdown. Those are different contracts, and one annotation should not be assumed to control all of them.

followups.q: Should registration order select the default implementation?
followups.a: No. Use explicit candidate selection such as qualifiers or a primary bean where that matches the requirement.

followups.q: Can ordered startup tasks still fail?
followups.a: Yes. Ordering does not add retries, readiness guarantees or rollback across startup side effects.

questions.trap: Assuming an ordered list, singleton initialization and lifecycle start order are interchangeable concepts.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; separate from candidate resolution and bean lifecycle timing already covered.

questions.question: How would you make an optional connector enabled only by an explicit configuration property?
questions.answer: I would place the connector configuration behind an explicit property condition, with a clear prefix, property name, expected value and missing-value policy. For a boolean opt-in, specifying havingValue as true avoids treating arbitrary non-false strings as an enablement signal under the annotation's default matching rule. The rest of the application must also tolerate the bean being absent, through an optional capability boundary rather than an unconditional dependency that fails startup. These conditions are normally evaluated when the context builds; changing a property afterward does not dynamically create or destroy the bean. A runtime feature toggle needs a separate request-time decision and a policy for work already in flight.

followups.q: What cases should the configuration test cover?
followups.a: Missing, explicitly false, explicitly true and malformed values, plus the behavior of consumers when the connector is absent.

followups.q: Is disabling a bean equivalent to revoking authorization?
followups.a: No. Feature availability and authorization are separate controls; neither should be inferred from the other.

questions.trap: Expecting a startup bean condition to behave like a live feature flag without a refresh or runtime decision mechanism.
questions.notes: Unverified proposed connector wiring. No specific existing feature-flag integration is claimed.

questions.question: How would you test auto-configuration backoff without launching the whole web application?
questions.answer: For a focused Boot configuration test I would use ApplicationContextRunner with just the configuration under test and its required collaborators. I can supply properties and user configuration, then assert which beans exist, which do not, and whether startup failed. To test backoff, one case has no user implementation and expects the default; another supplies a user bean and verifies the default does not create an unwanted duplicate. Additional cases can cover missing classes or disabled properties. The runner closes the context after its callback, reducing lifecycle leaks between tests. It checks container wiring rather than replacing business-unit tests or proving that a deployed server and its external dependencies work together.

followups.q: Would a mock-only unit test catch a missing bean definition?
followups.a: Usually not. It bypasses container construction, so wiring needs a context-level test.

followups.q: Why assert absence as well as presence?
followups.a: An extra default bean can create ambiguous injection or allocate unwanted resources even when the expected user bean exists.

questions.trap: Calling a plain Java object test proof that conditional Spring wiring is correct.
questions.notes: Unverified test strategy; no Spring test execution claimed and no unexecuted snippet included.

questions.question: Does editing a mounted configuration file automatically update an already bound @ConfigurationProperties object?
questions.answer: Not in a plain Boot application merely because the file changed. Startup loading and binding are not an automatic continuous file-watching and rebinding service. I would identify the actual refresh mechanism, if one is installed, and which beans or clients it replaces or updates. Even with refresh support, changing a settings object does not prove an already constructed connection pool or HTTP client adopted the new values. Some changes are safer through a rolling restart with validated configuration. For true live updates, I need validation before publication, consistent snapshots for readers and a policy for in-flight operations using the previous version. Secret rotation also requires coordination with the external provider, not just local field changes.

followups.q: Does adding @Value create file watching?
followups.a: No. Property injection alone does not define a refresh lifecycle.

followups.q: What should happen if the new configuration is invalid?
followups.a: Reject or fail the change according to policy; do not partially publish a mixture of old and invalid settings.

questions.trap: Equating an updated file on disk with a verified live reconfiguration of all dependent components.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. No Spring Cloud refresh capability is assumed to exist in the application.

questions.question: Why can independently upgrading one Spring library break an application managed by a Spring Boot release?
questions.answer: A Boot release manages a coordinated dependency set through its dependency management. Overriding one library can produce a mixture that compiles but fails at runtime when related libraries expect different methods, classes or behavior. I would inspect the resolved dependency graph, not only the versions written directly in the build file, and distinguish runtime dependencies from build plugins. A targeted override may be necessary for a security fix, but it needs compatibility review and focused startup and integration tests. Upgrading to an appropriate maintained Boot release is often a cleaner path than accumulating overrides. The dependency-management file constrains versions; it does not by itself add every managed library to the application.

followups.q: Does adding the Boot BOM enable every starter?
followups.a: No. It manages versions for dependencies that are actually included; dependency inclusion is separate.

followups.q: Is NoSuchMethodError usually a Java syntax problem?
followups.a: No. It often signals a mismatch between the API used at compilation and the class loaded at runtime; inspect the resolved and packaged artifacts.

questions.trap: Treating a successful compile as sufficient proof that a manually mixed framework dependency set is compatible.
questions.notes: Unverified upgrade strategy. No claim about current latest versions or particular security fixes.

questions.question: During a Boot 2 to Boot 3 migration, why is replacing every javax import with jakarta incorrect?
questions.answer: Boot 3 builds on Spring Framework 6 and Jakarta EE APIs, so affected enterprise APIs such as Servlet and Persistence use jakarta packages. But javax is also used by Java SE APIs, such as javax.sql and javax.crypto, which did not all move. A blanket text replacement can therefore corrupt valid imports. I would align the framework and third-party dependency versions first, then migrate the APIs that actually changed, including generated code and library integrations. Boot 3 also requires at least Java 17, while this handbook assumes Java 21. A namespace edit alone does not cover changes in security configuration, persistence behavior or deprecated APIs, so focused integration and regression tests remain necessary.

followups.q: Can an old servlet library work merely by adding jakarta.servlet?
followups.a: Not automatically. A library compiled against javax.servlet expects different types and generally needs a compatible release or deliberate migration.

followups.q: Does the minimum Java version identify the best production version?
followups.a: No. Choose a supported runtime compatible with the exact framework release and operational requirements, then test that combination.

questions.trap: Mechanically replacing the entire javax namespace and assuming the resulting application is fully migrated.
questions.notes: Unverified interview pattern. Stable Boot 3 baseline facts only, not a complete minor-version migration guide.

questions.question: Why might a bean exist in one ApplicationContext but remain invisible to another?
questions.answer: A bean belongs to a container, not a universal registry for the JVM. In a parent-child hierarchy, a child can generally resolve dependencies from its parent, but a parent cannot look down into child definitions and siblings do not automatically share their beans. A child can also have local definitions that affect resolution, so the context doing the lookup matters. This can explain differences between a servlet-specific context, a root context or separate test contexts. I would identify where each definition was registered and which context constructs the failing consumer. Starting another context to obtain the missing bean can duplicate resources and mask the wiring problem instead of fixing the intended ownership boundary.

followups.q: Are same-named singletons in separate contexts necessarily the same object?
followups.a: No. Singleton identity is scoped to the owning bean definition and container, subject to lookup through any configured hierarchy.

followups.q: Should a missing-bean investigation include context ownership?
followups.a: Yes, especially in multi-context deployments or tests where the definition exists but not in the consumer's visible context.

questions.trap: Assuming any bean created anywhere in the JVM is available to every Spring-managed consumer.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern. Does not assume Harsh uses a multi-context deployment.

questions.question: A singleton uses a request-scoped collaborator successfully in HTTP requests but fails in a scheduled job. Why?
questions.answer: A scoped proxy can be injected into a longer-lived singleton, but it still needs an active request scope when it resolves the actual target. A scheduled job normally has no HTTP request context, so accessing that dependency can fail at execution time. The proxy solves the difference in bean lifetime; it does not manufacture a request for every caller. I would separate request extraction from reusable business behavior and pass the required tenant or user data explicitly as an immutable value where appropriate. Capturing a live request-scoped object for later asynchronous work is also unsafe because the original request can finish first. Background work needs its own valid identity and resource lifecycle.

followups.q: Does making the request data globally static solve it?
followups.a: No. That risks sharing one user's data with unrelated requests and does not establish valid background authorization.

followups.q: Can a provider eliminate the need for an active request?
followups.a: No. Deferred lookup changes when resolution happens, not whether the required scope exists at that time.

questions.trap: Assuming successful injection of a scoped proxy proves that the target is valid in every future execution context.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; scope activation is distinct from logging or security-context propagation in S05.

questions.question: What happens between calling SpringApplication.run and the application accepting requests?
questions.answer: Startup is a sequence, not one instant. Boot prepares the environment, creates and refreshes an application context, registers and instantiates required beans, and completes configured startup callbacks before reporting readiness. A web server is created as part of that process, but a listening socket alone does not prove the service is ready for useful traffic. Failures in bean creation or startup runners can abort startup. I would distinguish process started, server accepting connections, and readiness for the intended workload, then investigate the earliest causal exception rather than the last wrapper message.

followups.q: Can a runner fail startup?
followups.a: Yes. An uncaught startup-runner failure can prevent successful application startup.

followups.q: Does a bound port prove readiness?
followups.a: No. The process may still be initializing or unable to satisfy its service contract.

questions.trap: Treating a successful TCP connection as proof that initialization and dependencies are healthy.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How does ApplicationContext add to the basic BeanFactory role?
questions.answer: BeanFactory is the fundamental container contract for retrieving and managing beans. ApplicationContext builds on that role with broader application infrastructure, including event publication, message resolution and integration with environment and resource facilities. In ordinary Boot applications I normally depend on the context-level application rather than manually constructing a bare factory. Both are containers, and the difference is not that one performs dependency injection while the other does not. When investigating behavior, I identify the concrete context implementation and its registered infrastructure instead of assuming every optional capability exists in every minimal container setup.

followups.q: Does a BeanFactory lack dependency injection?
followups.a: No. It provides the core bean creation and dependency wiring contract.

followups.q: Should application services depend on the container directly?
followups.a: Usually not; explicit constructor dependencies keep business code easier to construct and test.

questions.trap: Describing the interfaces as unrelated or claiming dependency injection exists only in ApplicationContext.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What does a Spring FactoryBean contribute, and how do you distinguish it from an ordinary bean factory method?
questions.answer: A FactoryBean is itself a managed bean whose contract supplies another object as the product exposed for normal lookup by its bean name. This is useful when a framework needs to construct a product through specialized logic, such as a proxy or resource abstraction. The factory and its product are distinct identities and may have different lifecycle considerations. An @Bean method is simpler when ordinary explicit construction is enough: it returns the object that becomes the bean. I would use FactoryBean only when that indirection is meaningful, because lookup and diagnostics can otherwise surprise maintainers.

followups.q: How can code request the factory itself?
followups.a: Spring provides a special dereference form using an ampersand prefix for FactoryBean lookup.

followups.q: Does every factory-created object need FactoryBean?
followups.a: No. A configuration @Bean factory method is usually clearer for direct construction.

questions.trap: Assuming the registered FactoryBean instance and the object normally injected under its name are necessarily the same object.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: When would you use @Import instead of component scanning to register configuration?
questions.answer: Component scanning is convenient when an application owns a package of stereotyped components and the scan boundary is intentional. @Import makes a configuration dependency explicit: one configuration can include another configuration class or selected component without broadening package discovery. That is useful for modular configuration and library integration, where silently scanning unrelated classes would be surprising. Neither mechanism should be used to register arbitrary classes without considering their dependencies and conditions. I would test the resulting context boundary and make optional modules opt in deliberately, so adding a class to a package does not accidentally change production wiring.

followups.q: Does @Import recursively scan every package?
followups.a: No. It imports the declared configuration or selector behavior; scanning remains a separate mechanism.

followups.q: Can an imported configuration define beans?
followups.a: Yes. Its configuration declarations are processed as part of the importing context.

questions.trap: Assuming an imported class and a package scan have identical discovery scope.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: A component is annotated correctly but is not registered. What determines the default scan boundary?
questions.answer: The application configuration that enables component scanning establishes which packages are considered, and Boot's usual application arrangement derives a default boundary from the package containing its main configuration class. A stereotype does not make a class globally discoverable. I would check the class's fully qualified package, the effective scan base packages, active configuration and any include or exclude filters. Moving the application class can therefore change registration without changing the component. I prefer a coherent package layout or an explicit, narrow scan declaration over scanning the entire classpath, which can create accidental beans and confusing startup failures.

followups.q: Will @Component work outside the scan path?
followups.a: Not by itself; use an explicit import or suitable scan configuration to register it.

followups.q: Why avoid scanning every package?
followups.a: It can pick up unintended components and make ownership and startup behavior harder to reason about.

questions.trap: Adding more stereotypes when the actual defect is that the class lies outside every registration boundary.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates. Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 5.2 (Accolite).

questions.question: What trade-off does enabling lazy bean initialization introduce?
questions.answer: Lazy initialization delays creation of eligible beans until they are first needed. It can shorten initial work when many optional components are unused, but it also moves construction failures and resource allocation to a later request or execution path. A health check may look successful before a rarely used bean has ever been created. I would measure startup benefit, identify which beans are truly optional, and ensure first-use latency and failure handling are acceptable. Lazy creation does not solve a missing dependency or a bad graph; it can simply postpone evidence of the defect until production traffic reaches that path.

followups.q: Does lazy initialization remove a broken dependency?
followups.a: No. It changes when creation is attempted, not whether the dependency can be resolved.

followups.q: Should every bean be lazy?
followups.a: No. Critical wiring may be better validated during startup so failures surface before traffic arrives.

questions.trap: Calling delayed bean creation a fix for startup errors without considering when the same error will appear.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: When is @DependsOn justified, and what does it not replace?
questions.answer: @DependsOn expresses an initialization or destruction ordering dependency that is not already represented by a bean reference. It can be appropriate when one managed component must initialize before another because of an external side effect or shared resource contract. It does not inject the named bean, make a missing dependency available, or establish a general order for unrelated beans. If a component genuinely uses another component, I prefer an explicit constructor dependency because it documents both ordering and collaboration. I treat DependsOn as a narrow lifecycle declaration and test shutdown behavior too, since inverse destruction ordering can matter when one component relies on another during cleanup.

followups.q: Does it make the dependency injectable?
followups.a: No. It expresses ordering; declare an injection point separately if the bean is used.

followups.q: Does it order every bean in the context?
followups.a: No. It applies to the declared dependency relationship, not a global sequence.

questions.trap: Using ordering metadata instead of declaring a real collaborator or assuming it controls all startup work.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What kind of task belongs in a BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor?
questions.answer: A BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor is an early container extension point for inspecting or registering bean definitions before ordinary bean instantiation. It extends the factory-post-processing phase with access to the registry itself, so it can add definitions that later processing and bean creation will use. That power also makes timing sensitive: fetching application objects from this early callback can instantiate them before all post-processors are installed. I would prefer declarative configuration or imports for normal application wiring and reserve registry mutation for framework-level cases. The test should inspect definitions and startup behavior, not rely on incidental construction order of business services.

followups.q: Does it operate on fully initialized bean instances?
followups.a: No. Its principal work is on definitions during early container setup.

followups.q: Should ordinary services register themselves this way?
followups.a: Usually not; stereotypes and configuration methods are simpler and more maintainable.

questions.trap: Treating early registry callbacks as a convenient place to call getBean for application logic.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: Why are infrastructure post-processors often declared through static @Bean methods?
questions.answer: BeanFactoryPostProcessor and BeanPostProcessor instances participate in creating and modifying other beans, so Spring must discover them early. A non-static factory method can require its containing configuration object to be instantiated too soon, potentially causing premature creation and incomplete processing warnings for that configuration or its dependencies. A static @Bean method can create the processor without first instantiating the configuration class. I keep such methods narrowly dependent on infrastructure values and avoid injecting ordinary application services into processors. This is a lifecycle ordering concern, not a stylistic rule to make every @Bean method static.

followups.q: Should all factory methods be static?
followups.a: No. The concern is early infrastructure processors; ordinary bean factories can use normal configuration dependencies.

followups.q: What warning can reveal premature creation?
followups.a: Startup may report beans not eligible for full post-processing, indicating they were created before all processors were ready.

questions.trap: Assuming processor beans have the same safe creation timing as ordinary application components.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How do initialization callbacks relate to dependency injection and bean post-processing?
questions.answer: Spring first constructs the bean and populates its dependencies, then applies relevant pre-initialization processing, invokes initialization callbacks, and applies post-initialization processing. The resulting reference used by consumers can therefore be a processed or wrapped object rather than the raw instance. Initialization callbacks are intended for local setup after dependencies are available, not for arbitrary application startup orchestration or long blocking work. Multiple callback mechanisms can make ordering less obvious, so I choose one clear lifecycle approach and verify actual behavior through a focused context test when ordering matters. Destruction callbacks are a separate phase and depend on the bean's managed lifecycle.

followups.q: Are dependencies available in the constructor?
followups.a: Constructor parameters are available during construction; field and setter dependencies are populated afterward.

followups.q: Does a manually created object receive callbacks?
followups.a: Not automatically; the container must manage the instance through its lifecycle.

questions.trap: Putting whole-application readiness work in a bean callback and assuming it runs after every component is ready.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What should a Spring bean's destruction callback own, and when might it not run?
questions.answer: A destruction callback should release resources owned by that managed bean, such as a locally created handle that requires explicit closure. The container can invoke configured destruction behavior when its context is closed cleanly, but abrupt process termination cannot be treated as a guaranteed callback. Prototype instances are a notable ownership case: after handing one to a caller, Spring does not normally track its complete destruction lifecycle. I would use appropriate closeable-resource patterns, make cleanup safe to repeat where practical, and keep durable business completion out of shutdown callbacks. Shutdown hooks complement operational termination handling; they are not a substitute for external recovery of interrupted work.

followups.q: Will cleanup always run after a machine crash?
followups.a: No. A crash can stop the process before callbacks execute, so external resources need their own expiry or recovery policy.

followups.q: Does Spring close every prototype automatically?
followups.a: No. The caller generally owns cleanup after receiving a prototype instance.

questions.trap: Assuming process termination reliably completes arbitrary business work through @PreDestroy.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How would you manage cleanup when a prototype bean owns a resource?
questions.answer: Prototype scope controls creation: Spring supplies a new instance for each request to the container, but it does not retain ordinary singleton-style tracking for the product's eventual destruction. If that instance owns a file handle or other closeable resource, the component requesting it must have an explicit cleanup contract. I would consider whether a try-with-resources factory or a narrower method-scoped resource is clearer than a prototype bean at all. ObjectProvider can request an instance when needed, but it does not transfer cleanup responsibility back to the container. I document who closes the object and test that every success and failure path does so.

followups.q: Does requesting through ObjectProvider change destruction behavior?
followups.a: No. It changes lookup timing, not ownership of the returned prototype's cleanup.

followups.q: Could a singleton be simpler?
followups.a: Yes, if the resource is safely reusable and its lifecycle truly matches the context lifetime.

questions.trap: Assuming every bean obtained from the container will automatically receive a destruction callback when no longer referenced.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What does SmartInitializingSingleton signal that an ordinary initialization callback does not?
questions.answer: SmartInitializingSingleton provides a callback after the container has instantiated all regular non-lazy singletons during context startup. That makes it useful for infrastructure that needs to inspect the completed singleton set, rather than a bean-local callback that runs while other singleton creation may still be underway. It does not mean every lazy bean has been created, nor does it mean the web service is operationally ready for all traffic. I would avoid turning the callback into a hidden application-wide task runner; use the lifecycle contract that matches the requirement and keep any work bounded. If it affects readiness, make that relationship explicit and observable.

followups.q: Does it guarantee lazy singletons exist?
followups.a: No. Its meaning concerns regular singleton pre-instantiation, not every deferred bean.

followups.q: Is it a replacement for a runner?
followups.a: Not generally; a runner communicates application startup work more directly.

questions.trap: Reading 'all singletons' as every bean of every scope and a guarantee of full application readiness.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What problem does @Lookup method injection solve, and what constraints would you check?
questions.answer: @Lookup lets Spring override a method on a managed bean so each invocation resolves a bean from the container, commonly for a shorter-lived dependency needed by a singleton. It avoids storing a single prototype reference during singleton construction. Because the technique depends on runtime subclassing, the containing type and lookup method must be suitable for that mechanism, and manually constructed instances will not receive the override. I would compare it with injecting ObjectProvider or an explicit factory; those make lookup visible in ordinary Java and are often simpler to test. Use lookup injection only when its container-managed method semantics provide a real benefit.

followups.q: Does @Lookup work on a manually created object?
followups.a: No. The container must create and enhance the managed instance for the lookup method behavior.

followups.q: What alternative exposes the lookup explicitly?
followups.a: Inject ObjectProvider or a domain-specific factory and request the object at the needed point.

questions.trap: Expecting a plain new instance or a method that cannot be overridden to perform container lookups.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: When is ObjectProvider a useful alternative to making a dependency optional with nullable injection?
questions.answer: ObjectProvider makes container lookup an explicit operation that can happen later, and it offers methods for optional resolution or obtaining an instance when needed. That is useful when a dependency is genuinely optional, when a shorter-lived bean must be requested from a longer-lived consumer, or when resolving it during construction would create an unnecessary cycle. It also couples the consumer to Spring's container API, so I would not use it to hide an ordinary required collaborator. A provider does not make an absent bean available or ensure the requested scope is active. I test both present and missing configurations and keep the fallback behavior intentional.

followups.q: Should a mandatory service use a provider just in case?
followups.a: Usually no; constructor injection communicates that the collaborator is required and fails early.

followups.q: Can provider lookup fix every circular dependency?
followups.a: No. It may defer resolution, but the dependency graph and first-use behavior still need to be valid.

questions.trap: Using deferred lookup as a way to make a required dependency's startup failure disappear without designing its eventual failure path.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How do Spring profiles differ from a runtime feature flag?
questions.answer: Profiles conditionally include bean definitions or configuration when the application context is built. They are useful for selecting environment-specific infrastructure or configuration, but changing an active profile is not ordinarily a request-time decision that swaps behavior safely in a running context. A feature flag is evaluated according to an application's runtime policy and can be targeted or changed independently when that system supports it. I would not use profiles as authorization controls or assume a profile name proves the deployment is production-safe. Keep configuration selection, user eligibility and security decisions separate, and test the exact active-profile combination used by each deployment.

followups.q: Can profiles enforce user-specific behavior?
followups.a: No. Profiles select application configuration, not per-user access rights.

followups.q: Can multiple profiles be active?
followups.a: Yes, so assess how their definitions combine and whether they create ambiguity.

questions.trap: Treating environment profiles as live feature switches or security boundaries.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What would you check when two profile-specific configurations unexpectedly load together?
questions.answer: I would inspect the effective active profiles and every profile condition contributing the candidate definitions. Profiles can be composed, inherited or activated by deployment inputs, so seeing one expected name does not mean it is the only active one. I then identify whether the competing beans are both registered and whether the consumer expects one or a collection. The repair may be a narrower profile expression, explicit candidate selection, or a configuration layout that prevents incompatible modules from loading together. I validate the actual deployment property set in a focused context test, rather than relying on a developer machine's default profile.

followups.q: Does @Profile select only one bean automatically?
followups.a: No. Multiple matching definitions can be registered, and normal dependency resolution still applies.

followups.q: Where should the effective profile be checked?
followups.a: In the running process environment and deployment configuration, with sensitive diagnostics protected.

questions.trap: Assuming the profile written on one configuration excludes every other configuration by default.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: Why can the same property have different values in a test, local run and deployed process?
questions.answer: Spring resolves values from an Environment composed of property sources, and each execution may supply a different set of files, profiles, environment variables, command-line arguments or test overrides. The same key can therefore resolve differently without the packaged file changing. I would inspect the process inputs and identify the winning source for that key, while keeping secret values redacted. Tests should state their properties explicitly so they do not accidentally inherit workstation state. I avoid relying on an undocumented assumption about precedence; for a version-sensitive ordering detail, I check the selected Boot reference and the running environment's origin diagnostics. [VERIFY: Spring Boot reference for property-source precedence in the selected Boot minor version]

followups.q: Should a test depend on a developer's environment variable?
followups.a: No. Declare required values in the test setup so it is reproducible.

followups.q: Can diagnostics reveal secrets?
followups.a: Yes. Protect access and verify sanitization before exposing configuration origins.

questions.trap: Assuming the value in application.properties is necessarily the effective value in every environment.
verify: [VERIFY: Spring Boot reference for property-source precedence in the selected Boot minor version]
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; precedence ordering is intentionally not asserted; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How would you reason about a configuration file imported from another property file?
questions.answer: I would identify which configuration loader processes the import, whether the imported resource is optional, and which profile or deployment inputs activate the importing document. An import adds another source to effective configuration; it does not prove that the file exists in every packaging or runtime environment. I would check startup diagnostics for missing-resource and binding failures, then test the expected file-present and file-absent cases. Exact import syntax and precedence can vary with the Boot configuration mechanism and release, so I would verify the selected minor-version reference rather than generalize from an older application.properties example. Secret-bearing sources also need protected access and logging. [VERIFY: Spring Boot Config Data import syntax and precedence for the selected Boot minor version]

followups.q: Does an optional import validate required settings?
followups.a: No. Validate the bound configuration separately so an omitted file cannot silently leave unsafe values.

followups.q: Can a local file prove the production artifact contains it?
followups.a: No. Inspect the packaged resources and deployment mount or source configuration.

questions.trap: Assuming an imported file is present and loaded merely because it exists in the developer's checkout.
verify: [VERIFY: Spring Boot Config Data import syntax and precedence for the selected Boot minor version]
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; version-sensitive import details require reference verification; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What does relaxed binding mean for a @ConfigurationProperties field name?
questions.answer: Relaxed binding lets supported property-name forms map to a canonical configuration property, so environment-oriented uppercase and underscore names can bind to a structured Java property without manually reading strings. It is a binder feature, not permission to invent arbitrary aliases or ignore the documented naming rules. I define a stable prefix, use clear kebab-case property names in files, and test the external form actually used by deployment. If a value is unexpectedly absent, I inspect the target type, registration, source name and binding diagnostics. I do not log sensitive bound values while diagnosing a name mismatch.

followups.q: Does relaxed binding convert every misspelling?
followups.a: No. Supported normalization is constrained; misspelled properties can remain unbound or be rejected under strict validation.

followups.q: Why keep a configuration prefix?
followups.a: It groups ownership and prevents unrelated settings from colliding.

questions.trap: Treating relaxed binding as fuzzy matching that makes arbitrary property typos harmless.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: Why bind timeouts as Duration instead of an unqualified integer?
questions.answer: A Duration makes the unit part of the configuration value instead of leaving readers to guess whether an integer means milliseconds, seconds or minutes. The binder can convert supported textual forms into a typed duration, and validation can reject zero, negative or unreasonable values according to the application's contract. I also distinguish connection timeout, response timeout and an overall operation deadline; similarly named values are not interchangeable. I test representative configuration forms against the selected Boot version and avoid silently choosing a default that can make a remote call wait indefinitely. The configuration owner should document the operational meaning, not just the Java type.

followups.q: Does one timeout setting bound an entire multi-step operation?
followups.a: Not necessarily; each client and retry step may have its own timeout unless an end-to-end deadline is enforced.

followups.q: Should zero mean no timeout?
followups.a: Only if the API explicitly defines that meaning; reject ambiguous values rather than relying on accidental library behavior.

questions.trap: Using an unexplained integer and assuming every downstream API interprets it in the same unit.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How should invalid Boot configuration fail, and where should validation live?
questions.answer: Configuration validation should reject impossible or unsafe values before the application begins serving requests. I model related settings in a typed properties object, express local constraints such as required fields and positive limits, and add cross-field checks when two individually valid values form an invalid combination. Registration and validation infrastructure must actually be active; annotations alone do not guarantee validation. Failure output should identify the property and constraint without printing a secret. I test missing, boundary and contradictory values in a context-level configuration test. For policies that require a remote service check, I separate the remote availability decision from simple structural validation.

followups.q: Should an invalid required endpoint silently use localhost?
followups.a: No. A plausible fallback can hide a deployment error and direct production traffic incorrectly.

followups.q: Can validation prove a downstream is reachable?
followups.a: No. Structural validation and runtime dependency health are separate checks.

questions.trap: Assuming a validation annotation is enforced without registering and validating the properties bean.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What are the practical advantages and constraints of immutable configuration properties?
questions.answer: Immutable configuration gives consumers a stable snapshot: once constructed, a caller cannot casually mutate a timeout or endpoint that other beans assumed would remain constant. Constructor binding also makes required values visible at creation and can support final fields and nested value types. It does not automatically make a live refresh atomic or update clients already constructed from those values. The configuration type still needs the appropriate Boot registration and validation. I choose immutability for startup configuration whose values should remain fixed, and use an explicit refresh design only when runtime changes are a real requirement, including safe publication and consistent behavior for in-flight operations.

followups.q: Does changing an immutable object update a client built from it?
followups.a: No. The client must have an explicit reconstruction or refresh mechanism.

followups.q: Is immutability useful for tests?
followups.a: Yes. Tests can construct a clear value and avoid hidden mutation between cases.

questions.trap: Equating an immutable properties object with automatic live configuration refresh.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: When would you add a converter for a custom configuration value?
questions.answer: A converter is useful when a configuration value has a well-defined textual representation but should be exposed to application code as a domain type, such as a validated identifier or a structured endpoint value. I define parsing rules, reject malformed input with a useful property-oriented error, and keep conversion free of remote side effects. A custom converter should not turn configuration binding into a hidden network lookup. I test valid, boundary and invalid strings using the same registration path the application uses, since a converter that exists in a test helper but is not installed in Boot will not help production binding.

followups.q: Should conversion contact the database?
followups.a: No. Binding should be deterministic and bounded, not depend on remote state.

followups.q: What if the value format changes?
followups.a: Version and migrate the configuration contract deliberately, with tests for supported and rejected forms.

questions.trap: Writing a parser that accepts ambiguous values or performs side effects during context creation.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How should a library's default bean yield to an application's custom implementation?
questions.answer: A library configuration can conditionally provide a default when no matching application bean is already defined. The condition should target the intended type or bean contract and be placed so user definitions are visible when the decision is evaluated. I would define what counts as a replacement, including whether subclasses or multiple candidates should suppress the default, instead of assuming any custom bean disables all library configuration. A focused context test should cover default-only, user-override and ambiguous-candidate cases. If the library is meant to be reusable, its configuration should avoid scanning the host application's packages or taking control of unrelated bean names.

followups.q: Does one user bean disable every auto-configuration?
followups.a: No. Backoff is scoped to the particular condition and bean contract.

followups.q: Should the default share a bean name with the user bean?
followups.a: Avoid relying on name replacement; use an explicit condition and compatibility test.

questions.trap: Claiming that defining any application bean globally turns off Boot defaults.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How would you test the absent, disabled and enabled cases of an optional integration bean?
questions.answer: I test the condition as a small matrix rather than only the happy path: property missing, explicitly disabled, enabled, and malformed or unsupported values. For each context I assert whether the integration bean exists and whether its consumers remain valid when it does not. If the condition also depends on a class being present, I test that boundary separately. ApplicationContextRunner is suitable for focused Boot configuration tests because it lets the test supply properties and user definitions without launching a full server. These checks validate wiring only; they do not prove the remote integration works or that production credentials are correct.

followups.q: Is bean absence enough to test?
followups.a: No. Exercise consumers to ensure optional capability absence is an intentional supported state.

followups.q: Does this test verify a real remote service?
followups.a: No. It checks context configuration, not deployed integration behavior.

questions.trap: Testing only the enabled case and missing the ambiguous or broken default behavior when configuration is absent.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; no code execution or integration test is claimed; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: Why can adding a dependency unexpectedly change which Boot configuration activates?
questions.answer: Auto-configuration can be conditional on classes being present, so changing the resolved runtime classpath can make a configuration eligible that was previously absent. A transitive dependency may therefore affect bean definitions even when application source did not change. I would compare the resolved dependency graph and the condition evaluation output for both builds, then verify which candidate beans were created. The right response may be dependency alignment, an explicit property, or a deliberate exclusion, depending on the intent. I avoid assuming that a library listed in the build file is harmless merely because application code does not import it directly.

followups.q: Does compile scope alone prove runtime presence?
followups.a: No. Inspect the packaged runtime graph and deployment artifact.

followups.q: Should every unexpected configuration be excluded immediately?
followups.a: No. First confirm why it matched and whether the dependency is required.

questions.trap: Debugging source annotations while ignoring that the dependency graph changed the available conditional classes.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: When is excluding a Boot auto-configuration appropriate, and how do you avoid masking the cause?
questions.answer: An exclusion is appropriate when the application deliberately does not want a specific auto-configuration and supplies or intentionally omits the capability itself.
