Before excluding it, I inspect the condition report and the failing bean chain to understand why it matched and what it tried to create. An exclusion can hide a missing property, dependency conflict or mistaken application type until a later request fails. I document the reason near the configuration and add a context test that confirms the intended remaining beans. questions.question: How would you find which configuration class contributed an unexpected bean?
questions.answer: I start from the bean's type and name, then inspect its bean definition origin and whether it came from component scanning, an imported configuration, a factory method or auto-configuration. The condition report can show why an auto-configuration was eligible, while context diagnostics or a focused test can reveal the registered definition and its source. I compare active profiles and the resolved classpath if the bean appears only in one environment. I avoid deleting the bean by name before understanding its owner, because it may be a required infrastructure component. Once identified, I adjust the narrowest configuration condition and assert the resulting bean set in a test.

followups.q: Does a matching condition show the exact bean instance?
followups.a: Not necessarily; also inspect the bean definition and factory method that created it.

followups.q: What if it appears only in deployment?
followups.a: Compare deployed profiles, properties and runtime dependencies with the local environment.

questions.trap: Removing an unexpected bean without identifying which configuration owns it or what depends on it.

questions.question: How do you prevent development-only beans from entering a production context?
questions.answer: I place development-only configuration behind an explicit profile or condition and make production configuration selection part of the deployment contract. I do not rely on a developer's default profile or on a naming convention to exclude a bean. A deployment test or packaged-context test should activate the same profile inputs as production and assert that development stubs, permissive adapters and test credentials are absent. Profiles are configuration selection, not a security system, so production secrets and access controls still require independent enforcement. I also check whether imported configurations or test utilities register the bean through another path that bypasses the intended profile condition.

followups.q: Does naming a profile dev guarantee it is inactive in production?
followups.a: No. Verify the actual runtime profile inputs.

followups.q: Are profiles sufficient to protect secrets?
followups.a: No. Use proper secret management and access controls independently.

questions.trap: Assuming a bean is development-only because its class name or package says test.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; no deployment configuration is claimed; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: What can an ApplicationContextRunner test prove about a configuration module, and what remains untested?
questions.answer: A focused context runner can prove that a selected configuration registers or omits expected beans under chosen properties and user definitions, and that the context fails for invalid wiring. It is especially useful for conditional auto-configuration because each case starts with a small controlled environment. It does not prove that the production artifact includes the same dependencies, that an HTTP request traverses the server, or that a remote client can authenticate and communicate. I keep those as separate packaging, web and integration checks. The test is valuable precisely when its boundary is explicit and its assumptions match the configuration contract being checked.

followups.q: Does this prove the server starts?
followups.a: Only if the test configures the relevant web server path; a basic context runner does not.

followups.q: Does a bean-presence assertion prove it works?
followups.a: No. It proves registration, not downstream behavior or runtime correctness.

questions.trap: Calling a lightweight wiring test full application integration coverage.

questions.question: Why should configuration tests avoid depending on the developer's ambient environment?
questions.answer: Environment variables, system properties, active profiles and local files can silently supply values that make a test pass on one machine and fail in CI. A reproducible configuration test declares its required inputs and resets any process-wide state it changes. I also avoid embedding real credentials and assert that missing required values fail safely. For environment-specific behavior, I test named profiles or property sets explicitly rather than inheriting the workstation's active profile. This makes the test describe the application's contract and helps distinguish a wiring regression from a developer setup difference. The same principle applies to dependency versions and packaged resources.

followups.q: Should tests mutate global system properties?
followups.a: Only with scoped setup and reliable cleanup; prefer test-specific property mechanisms.

followups.q: Can a developer profile accidentally hide a production defect?
followups.a: Yes. Run explicit production-like configuration checks in CI.

questions.trap: Accepting a green local context test without knowing which external settings made it pass.

questions.question: What should Spring configuration do when a required secret is absent or malformed?
questions.answer: If a secret is essential to the service's declared capability, startup should fail through a clear validation path rather than silently substituting an empty or development value. The error should name the missing configuration key or expected format without echoing the secret. I check the secret provider's mount or injection contract, active environment and binding target, then verify rotation and access policies separately. Optional capabilities can be conditionally disabled only when their absence has a safe, explicit behavior. A local placeholder secret must never be accidentally packaged as production configuration. I test failure behavior with synthetic values and do not claim that binding proves the credential is accepted by its remote authority.

followups.q: Should a fake default password keep startup green?
followups.a: No. It can turn a deployment mistake into an insecure or confusing runtime failure.

followups.q: Does successful binding prove the secret is valid remotely?
followups.a: No. Authentication with the external provider is a separate integration check.

questions.trap: Logging the actual secret while trying to diagnose a missing or malformed credential.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; no credential or external authentication result is claimed; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: How do you decide whether a Boot property should have a default or be mandatory?
questions.answer: A default is appropriate when it is safe across the supported environments and its operational meaning is clear. A required endpoint, credential or safety limit should usually be validated rather than silently guessed. I distinguish convenience defaults from security-sensitive or environment-specific values, document units and ranges, and test both absent and explicitly supplied cases. Defaults in a library should be conservative and allow application override without surprising side effects. I also verify how a missing property behaves in the selected binding mechanism instead of relying on an annotation's default semantics. A valid default is not automatically a suitable production value.

followups.q: Should a production URL default to localhost?
followups.a: Usually not; it can route production traffic to an unintended local service.

followups.q: Does an annotation's default always mean the same thing across APIs?
followups.a: No. Verify the semantics of the specific binding or condition API.

questions.trap: Using a fallback that makes startup succeed while directing live traffic to an incorrect or insecure target.
questions.notes: Unverified pattern; round, frequency and level are estimates.

questions.question: Give a disciplined sequence for diagnosing a Boot configuration defect that appears only after deployment.
questions.answer: I first capture the earliest causal exception and identify whether the failure is definition discovery, condition selection, property binding or bean construction. Then I compare the deployed artifact, runtime dependency graph, active profiles and effective configuration sources with the known-good environment, redacting secrets. If auto-configuration is involved, I inspect its condition report; if a value is wrong, I trace its property origin. I reproduce the exact inputs in a focused context test, make the smallest configuration correction, and verify startup plus the affected behavior. I preserve the diagnosis as a regression check rather than adding broad exclusions or defaults that merely hide the deployment difference.

followups.q: What should be compared first across environments?
followups.a: The artifact, effective profiles, runtime dependencies and property sources relevant to the failing bean.

followups.q: Why not add a broad exclusion immediately?
followups.a: It can hide the real mismatch and remove required infrastructure.

questions.trap: Changing application code before confirming whether deployment supplied the same artifact and configuration inputs.

questions.question: What does Spring Boot add on top of the Spring Framework?
questions.answer: Spring Boot is an opinionated layer on top of Spring, not a replacement. The Spring Framework gives you the container, dependency injection, MVC, data access and AOP, but you wire and configure everything yourself and manage compatible dependency versions. Boot adds auto-configuration driven by the classpath and properties, starter dependencies with a managed version BOM, an embedded server so the application runs as an executable JAR, externalised configuration, and production tooling through Actuator. @SpringBootApplication combines @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration and @ComponentScan.

followups.q: What does @EnableAutoConfiguration do?
followups.a: It registers conditional configuration classes that apply when matching classes or properties are present and back off when you define your own beans.

followups.q: Can a Boot application be deployed as a WAR?
followups.a: Yes, by extending SpringBootServletInitializer and packaging as a WAR, though the executable JAR is the default.

questions.trap: Describing Boot as a different framework. It configures and packages Spring, it does not replace it.
